title: Blue rejuvenation
caption: The globular cluster Messier 3, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 3 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 34000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, G. Piotto et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows Messier 3, a globular cluster containing half a million stars. About eight billion years old, it ranks among the biggest and brightest globulars yet found.

Its real distinction is its large number of variable stars, which change in brightness over time. It has 274 so far, far more than any other globular cluster, with more still turning up. At least 170 are RR Lyrae variables, whose pulsation period is linked to their true brightness. Comparing true and apparent brightness gives their distance, so they act as standard candles.

The cluster also holds a relatively high number of blue stragglers, which stand out clearly. They appear youthful, outshining their neighbours and looking bluer, yet all of a globular cluster's stars are thought to have formed together. One explanation is that an old star gains mass, for example by stripping it from a nearby star, which turns it bluer and makes it seem younger than it is.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.78 x 2.43 arcminutes) and distance (34000 light years), the frame spans roughly 27 × 24 light-years. Its light set out about 34,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the brightness changes of variable stars only reveal themselves through repeated measurements.

explore: Messier 3 lies about 34,000 light-years away in the direction of the constellation Canes Venatici. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters.
alt: A dense globular cluster of stars, including a number of conspicuous blue stars.
